item.title: Energy Brief: India Starts Pivoting Away From Russian Oil as New US Sanctions Law Bites; Saudi Restarts East-West Pipeline
item.description:
Indian refiners are trimming Russian crude purchases just as a new US law authorizes 100% tariffs on major buyers, while Saudi Arabia restarts its East-West pipeline as the main workaround to the Strait of Hormuz disruption. Oil slid below $100 on Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within a week.
► India Eases Off Russian Crude Ahead of New US Sanctions Law India's imports of Russian crude fell 16. 5% in August and are expected to decline again in September, according to trade data cited in an OilPrice. com review of Reuters figures — even as Russia remains India's largest supplier. Why it matters: The US is now directly targeting the price break that anchored India's Russian oil purchases — the single biggest remaining buyer — threatening to turn a commercial arbitrage into a geopolitical liability just as New Delhi needs stable supply.
► Saudi Restarts East-West Pipeline, the Escape Hatch Around Hormuz Saudi Arabia has restarted its East-West oil pipeline, restoring at least some flow through the ~4 million bpd route to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, per Reuters sources reported by OilPrice. com. Why it matters: Restoring this inland route reduces Saudi dependence on Hormuz transit — but the slow return and continued tightness show how much resilience the Red Sea corridor has lost to drone strikes, and how fragile the normalization is.
► Iran Offers to Reopen Hormuz Within a Week, Oil Breaks Below $100 Iran has offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases pressure, including steps toward ending the military blockade of Iranian ports and halting operations in the strait, a senior Iranian official told Japan's Kyo Why it matters: The seven-day window is a concrete, time-bound negotiating position rather than a vague overture — it tests whether Washington will trade blockade relief for restored flows, and whether either side can afford the optics of appearing to blink first.
► Libya's Sharara Field Hit by Armed Group Blockade Crude production at Libya's largest oilfield, Sharara, has slumped after an armed military group closed a valve on the pipeline carrying crude to the Zawiya export port, Libya's National Oil Corporation said, per OilPrice. com's review. Why it matters: Libya's recurring militia blockades are a reminder that supply fragility is not confined to the Gulf — a 340,000 bpd field offline compounds the tightness and gives the market another reason to keep a risk premium built into prices.
► European Industry Feels the Squeeze as UK Gas Prices Force Idling Chemical giant INEOS is idling three plants in Hull, UK — Europe's last remaining world-scale Acetyls units — blaming natural gas prices now 12 times the US level and 8 times China's, per the company's statement and OilPrice. com. Why it matters: Strategic self-sufficiency is eroding in real time: high gas prices are shifting basic industrial production — including defense-critical materials — out of Europe, an economic consequence of the energy squeeze that outlasts any single market move.
■ The Bottom Line Today shows both halves of the supply equation working at once: Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within a week and Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline restart point toward normalization and dragged Brent below $100, while India's quiet pullback from Russian crude, Libya's Sharara blockade, and INEOS idling British plants show how quickly new disruptions and new sanctions dynamics keep the risk premium alive. The watch item is Washington's response to Iran's time-bound offer, and whether October loadings confirm India is really pivoting away from Russian barrels under the threat of the new US tariff authority.

item.title: Energy Brief: Trump Says Russia Has 'Lost Control' of Its Oil Industry, Plans to Confront Zelensky Over Refinery Strikes at NYC Meeting
item.description:
With the US president publicly criticizing Moscow on energy for the first time, refinery strikes on both the Russian and Iranian supply lines are now the dominant driver of global oil prices, alongside a diesel shortage expected to last into 2027.
► Trump Turns on Moscow Over Refinery Strikes US President Donald Trump has said Russia has 'lost control' of its oil industry, a rare public criticism of Moscow, ahead of an Oval Office-adjacent meeting with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in New York this week. Why it matters: It signals a hardening US position that Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure — not just Iranian supply — are now seen by the White House as a price problem Washington must address, putting energy policy at the center of US-Ukraine diplomacy.
► Global Diesel Shortage Set to Last Into 2027 A global diesel shortage fueled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine is unlikely to ease before next year, Reuters reports, citing storage market indicators and industry participants. Why it matters: Diesel is the workhorse fuel of the global economy; a shortage this persistent pushes up the cost of moving everything, sharpening the economic pain of both wars and raising the political stakes for any ceasefire that does not restore refining capacity.
► Oil Slips a Fourth Day as Hormuz Flows Improve Brent crude fell 1. 7% to $102. Why it matters: The slide shows markets are pricing in partial supply restoration — or at least the absence of escalation — through Hormuz, but the underlying structural deficit in refined products remains, keeping price downside limited.
► India's Coal Crisis: 74 Plants Critically Low Nearly 40% of India's coal-fired power plants are running with critically low fuel stocks, government data show, as electricity demand rises amid hotter El Niño-linked weather. Coal inventories at thermal plants fell to 22. Why it matters: For Asia's third-largest economy, a coal stockout risks rolling power cuts just as the diesel and LNG squeeze bites; it also underscores how India's energy security rests on a strained domestic logistics chain more than on imported fuel.
► Asian LNG Demand Falls Second Year as War Shrinks Gulf Supply Asian demand for liquefied natural gas is on track to decline for a second consecutive year, Reuters reports, as the war on Iran curtails Gulf exports, tightening availability and lifting prices to multi-year highs that cut consumption. Why it matters: Persistent Gulf supply loss is pushing Asian buyers to lock in alternative sources and rethink long-term contracts, reshaping the LNG trade map and strengthening the negotiating hand of non-Gulf exporters.
► Houthis Push to Cut Off Yemen's Red Sea Coast Houthi fighters are pushing to seize strategic mountain positions in Yemen to isolate the country's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government forces, according to The Vibes, citing Reuters. Why it matters: Though overshadowed by the Iran and Ukraine fronts, the Houthi push to consolidate the Red Sea coastline keeps a key global chokepoint under active threat and complicates any Red Sea shipping normalization.
■ The Bottom Line The day's story is the re-centering of energy policy inside the Russia-Ukraine war: Trump's public line that Moscow has 'lost control' of its oil industry and his plan to confront Zelensky over refinery strikes make Russian processing capacity — not just Iranian supply — a top-tier driver of global prices. Beneath that, a diesel shortage set to run into 2027, record fuel costs, India's coal crunch, and shrinking Asian LNG demand show the economic strain of both conflicts spreading well beyond the battlefields. A fourth-day retreat in Brent to $102 offers only modest relief while refined-product deficits persist.

item.title: Energy Brief: Global Supertanker Shortage Sends Freight Costs Soaring and Threatens Long-Haul Crude Trades; Ukraine Launches Largest-Ever Drone Attack on Moscow Energy Sites; Oil Slips to One-Week Low on Qatar-Brokered US-Iran Deal Hopes
item.description:
The war's second-order costs keep mounting: a shortage of available oil tankers is driving freight rates up and eroding the economics of the longer routes that replaced the Gulf chokepoint, while Ukraine's record drone assault on Moscow hit an oil refinery. Oil prices fell to a one-week low as Qatar's mediation and Treasury comments raised hopes of a US-Iran deal, even as Iran hardened its Hormuz messaging.
► A Supertanker Shortage Is Redrawing the Economics of the Post-Hormuz Oil Trade Shipping markets are emerging as the war's quiet bottleneck. Why it matters: Freight is becoming a separate constraint layered on top of supply disruption. Even if barrels are available, the tankers to move them on longer diversion routes are not — a cost that quietly raises the effective price of landed crude and complicates the 'business as usual' workaround the market had been pricing in.
► Oil Slips to a One-Week Low as Qatar Mediation Raises Deal Hopes Crude fell on Sunday evening, with Reuters reporting oil hit over a one-week low on hopes of a boost to diplomacy in the Iran war. Why it matters: The market is now trading the possibility of de-escalation seriously for the first time, with Qatar as the channel. But the pullback is tentative — prices remain elevated because actual Hormuz flows are still constrained, and any collapse in the talks would reverse the move quickly.
► Ukraine Launches Its Largest-Ever Drone Attack on Moscow, Hitting Energy Sites Ukraine mounted its biggest drone assault on the Russian capital, with BBC reporting hundreds of drones fired at Moscow and the DW reporting two people killed. Why it matters: Russian refined-fuel output and export capacity were already severely constrained, and a strike on Moscow's refining ring tightens the domestic and export picture further — an additional drag on a Russian fuel export market already down roughly 50% year-on-year, according to earlier OilPrice data.
► Tehran Balances Deal Hopes With Firm Hormuz Leverage Signaling Alongside the mediation track, Iran International reports Tehran is signaling its Hormuz leverage while Trump weighs Iran options, and The Korea Times reports Iran and the US trading threats after Houthi attacks escalated the regional conflict. Why it matters: Iran appears to be calibrating between de-escalation signaling for the market and keeping Hormuz as leverage for the actual negotiation. The gap between what Tehran says publicly and what it concedes via intermediaries will determine whether this becomes a genuine reopening or another stalled round.
► China Steps Into the Diesel Gap as Global Shortages Deepen China is increasingly supplying the diesel shortfall created by the war's shipping and refinery disruptions. OilPrice. com reported, citing Reuters and Chinese customs data, that China exported 6. 01 million tons of refined fuels in August, up 12. Why it matters: China is quietly profiting from and cushioning the global product shortage, exporting refined fuels into a market desperate for diesel while shoring up its own coal supply.
■ The Bottom Line The day's story is the war's cost shifting from headlines into the machinery of trade: a tanker shortage is squeezing the economics of the longer post-Hormuz routes even as oil prices slip on Qatar-brokered hopes of a US-Iran deal, and Ukraine reached Moscow's refining ring with its largest drone attack yet. Prices are down only tentatively — supply risk and freight tightness remain the floor, and the relief rally depends entirely on the mediation track actually delivering. Until Hormuz genuinely reopens, the market is trading a hope, not a fix.

President Trump says he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that Iran 'wants to make a deal,' teeing up a UN General Assembly push with Gulf leaders next week. Separately, a UN fact-finding mission found 'reasonable grounds' the US committed war crimes in two Iran strikes, even as oil slid to a one-week low on Saudi reroutes.
► Trump Claims Direct Talks With Iran Ahead of UN General Assembly Push President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that the Iranians 'want to make a deal,' declaring the war, which began on Feb. 28, is 'hopefully' nearing its end, Fox News reports. Why it matters: A real or perceived channel to Tehran — however fragile — repositions the US-Iran conflict a week before UNGA, where a face-to-face or leader-level contact could test whether the 'wants to make a deal' line holds beyond rhetoric. It also gives Trump a domestic off-ramp ahead of midterms focused on gas prices.
► UN Panel Finds 'Reasonable Grounds' of US War Crimes in Iran A UN fact-finding mission said Thursday it found 'reasonable grounds' to believe US forces committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran, and that Iran committed crimes against humanity, AP and Bloomberg report. Why it matters: The war-crimes finding gives critics and neutral capitals documentation to attach to the US campaign right as Trump seeks a negotiated exit, complicating the messaging of a deal and feeding domestic and international pressure over the conduct of the conflict.
► Oil Slides to One-Week Low as Saudi Arabia Reroutes Exports Through Oman Oil prices fell to a one-week low Thursday, with Brent settling at $104. 82 (down 1%) and WTI at $101. 91, after reports that Saudi Arabia was moving crude through Oman to offset its damaged east-west pipeline, Reuters and Fox News report. Why it matters: Saudi rerouting via Oman partly cushions the pipeline outage, but it also signals the kingdom is pushing more barrels through Hormuz — the very chokepoint Iran claims to control — tying Saudi supply security more tightly to US naval protection and to the fate of the diplomacy.
► US Approves $24.3 Billion F-35 Sale to Saudi Arabia The US State Department approved the sale of 48 F-35 stealth fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal worth $24. 3 billion, announced Thursday, Reuters and the Financial Times report. Why it matters: Approving the F-35 to Riyadh — during an active war with Iran — signals the US sees Saudi Arabia as its enduring regional security anchor regardless of how the Iran talks resolve, and gives Riyadh leverage it can use against Houthi and Iranian pressure on its energy infrastructure.
► ExxonMobil Nears Orinoco Return as the US Rush Into Venezuela Deepens US supermajor ExxonMobil is nearing a preliminary deal to invest in Venezuela's oil fields, with talks focused on the Petromonagas project in the Orinoco Belt, Mother Jones and World Energy News report. Why it matters: The rapid succession of deals — Chevron, then Continental/Hamm, now ExxonMobil — shows Washington's Venezuela pivot is consolidating quickly, pulling US majors into the world's largest reserves, and squeezing Chinese operators out of Orinoco assets as Caracas trades access for revenue under US military threat.
► LNG Price Surge Prices Out Asian Buyers, While Europe Faces a Lean Winter Asia is set for its weakest September LNG imports in eight years as high spot prices deter buyers in China and South Asia, while Europe keeps paying up, Reuters reports across two analyses. Why it matters: The crunch is being exported to Asia even as Europe 'is saved' — a reminder that the LNG market's pain is borne by price-sensitive emerging buyers in China and South Asia, reshaping who can afford energy in a war-driven supply squeeze with no obvious relief in sight.

item.title: Energy Brief: Continental Strikes Venezuela Orinoco Deal as Trump's Sanctions Pivot Takes Shape; Iraq Pushes OPEC for 6M bpd Baseline
item.description:
Oklahoma shale giant Continental Resources and investor Heeney Capital signed Venezuela deals Wednesday, marking the clearest move yet by US firms into the sanctioned country's energy sector. Separately, Iraq is pressing OPEC+ to raise its baseline to 6 million bpd citing reconstruction needs, while Brent slid below $105 as the Saudi East-West pipeline repair race dominates the market.
► Continental Resources, Heeney Capital Sign Venezuela Deals in Test of Trump's Sanctions Pivot Oklahoma-based Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA on Wednesday to operate and develop the Ayacucho 2 Block in the Orinoco Belt — a 126,000-acre area holding an estimated 30 billion barr Why it matters: This is the concrete, deal-level translation of a policy shift that had been mostly rhetoric: Washington is moving from sanctioning Venezuela's energy sector to brokering US corporate entry into it.
► Oil Slides Below $105 as Middle East Disruptions Ease, Saudi Pipeline Repair Race Looms Brent crude fell $1. 25, or 1. 22%, to $104. 62 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate declined $1. 16, or 1. 2%, to $101. Why it matters: The price is caught between two forces: headline-driven relief on the diplomatic/military side, and a hardening physical shortage as Saudi export capacity stays impaired. The East-West pipeline is the escape valve that lets the kingdom bypass the choked Red Sea and Hormuz routes — if it stays down, the slide below $105 could reverse quickly.
► Iraq Asks OPEC+ for a 6 Million bpd Baseline, Citing $400B Reconstruction Needs Iraq is seeking a 6 million bpd OPEC+ production baseline, up from its current 4. 431 million bpd, as Baghdad pursues an aggressive expansion of its oil industry despite severe export disruptions, Bloomberg reported and Yahoo Finance echoed. Why it matters: Iraq's demand lands at a delicate moment: OPEC+ is trying to stabilize prices near $100-plus while members eye how much they can pump once export routes reopen. If Iraq gets anywhere near a 6 million bpd baseline, it reshapes the alliance's spare-capacity math for years.
► OPEC Output Fell 900,000 bpd in August; Saudi Arabia Down to 6.98 Million bpd OPEC crude output dropped 900,000 barrels per day in August, with Saudi Arabia's production falling over 1 million bpd to 6. 98 million bpd amid the chokepoint disruptions, according to cryptobriefing's tracking of OPEC data. Why it matters: This quantifies the war's real supply damage at the producer level: the kingdom is pumping at levels far below its installed capacity because it cannot ship. It underscores why the East-West pipeline repair is not just a market story but a national-output story, and why Iraq's quota ambitions look abstract while actual production is bottlenecked.
► Europe Spends Record €7.3bn on Russian Arctic Gas in Eight Months as Winter Squeeze Builds Europe has spent a record €7. 3 billion on Russian Arctic LNG in just eight months, surpassing the entire 2025 total, per an MSN review of trade data. Why it matters: The Yamal figure exposes a stubborn contradiction in Europe's energy posture: states sanction Russian oil while their utilities and shipping firms keep Arctic LNG flowing into the continent.

item.title: Energy Brief: Saudi Warns It Will Respond Firmly as Houthi Red Sea Blockade Draws Riyadh-Cairo Alliance; Oil Holds Near $107 as Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls
item.description:
Riyadh escalates its confrontation with the Houthis over control of the Bab el-Mandeb while Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman travels to Cairo for security backing. Simultaneously, the planned Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping talks are postponed and the tanker El Gaia becomes the flashpoint in a US-Iran blame war over who hit it — keeping Brent above $107.
► Saudi Arabia Vows 'Firm' Response as Houthi Maritime Blockade Tightens on the Red Sea Saudi Arabia on Tuesday warned it would react 'firmly' to Yemen's Houthi rebels after a series of ballistic missile and drone attacks wounded 13 civilians in the kingdom's south, according to The Hindu's live coverage of the West Asia war. Why it matters: With Hormuz still choked by the US-Iran war, the Houthi grip on Bab el-Mandeb closes off Saudi Arabia's alternative export route. The kingdom is now fighting a two-front energy war — and its Red Sea port of Yanbu, the escape valve for east-west pipeline flows, is directly in the firing line.
► Riyadh-Cairo Summit: MBS Seeks Egypt's Backing for Red Sea Security Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo and met President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for security talks after 13 people were injured by drone and missile attacks, the FT reported. Why it matters: Egypt is the quiet heavyweight in this conflict — its canal revenue collapse makes Cairo a vested stakeholder in reopening the Red Sea, and Riyadh is seeking an Arab-state front behind its campaign rather than acting alone. A coordinated Saudi-Egyptian posture on maritime security would reshape the regional response to the Houthi blockade.
► Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls: Iran-Oman Talks Postponed, El Gaia Becomes the Flashpoint Oman's foreign minister said the planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf nations on creating a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed, a setback reported by Reuters and the Associated Press. Why it matters: The postponed talks mean the shipping corridor that Gulf states and Iran had been circling remains unfilled, keeping Hormuz transit risk elevated.
► Oil Holds Near $107 as Hormuz Delay and Houthi Attacks Lift Prices Oil prices rose more than 3% on Monday as further Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, strikes affecting shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and the postponement of regional talks increased concerns about Middle East supply disruption, per Yahoo Finance. Why it matters: The market is now pricing in a prolonged, two-route supply problem rather than a single chokepoint. With the East-West pipeline down and Bab el-Mandeb contested on top of the Hormuz disruption, Saudi Arabia's ability to serve both its customer bases is structurally impaired — and the price reflects that there is no quick diplomatic fix in sight.

Why it matters: The war is now destroying demand faster than it is destroying supply — a dynamic that complicates price expectations. Even with severe supply losses, the demand-wipeout story means the market may not spiral as high as supply alone suggests, and both IEA and OPEC are signalling the economic pain of $100-plus crude is already suppressing consumption.
► Europe Braces for a Costly Winter: UK Bills Seen Jumping 25% Bloomberg Economics forecasts UK household energy bills will jump by about 25% in January as the Iran war drives up wholesale gas and electricity prices, adding to inflationary pressure. Why it matters: The war's inflation shock is now moving from oil markets into household bills in Europe and Asia.
